text:
The headphones were from my brother, which didn't surprise me. He was the sort of man who saw silence as something that could be purchased if you kept stacking up increments of three hundred dollars. I had them in the hospital corridor. The lights there are those bad fluorescents, the ones that hum like a wasp trapped in a tin cup. A janitor was out there too, his mop hitting the floor in this slow wet applause. I put the headphones on and the world went soft, and it felt like being underwater. Dad was in room 412. His breath was going in and out like a very shallow tide.
He was awake when I got in. His eyes followed me. It was the old look, the look of a man that doesn't trust his own memory. What are those, he said, pointing at them around my neck. I sat down in the vinyl chair next to him. Noise cancelling, I told him. Speak up, he said. I lifted the headphones up. Noise cancelling. He squinted at them. For the noise? Yes. He tried to smile. Only one side of his mouth did it. How? I turned them over. There are little ports in here. Microphones. They listen to the room. And then a chip in there takes the noise. Thousands of times a second it samples it. And it takes the sound wave and flips it upside down. Makes it a mirror image. Then the speakers play that flipped wave. And when they hit, they just cancel.
He said, A mirror image. So it's the noise meeting itself and disappearing. Exactly. He was looking up at the ceiling. There was a stain, it was spreading like a faded country. You make quiet by making more noise. That's either very smart or very sad. I laughed. I shouldn't have. It came out wrong. Both, I said. He went quiet. The tube for the oxygen was whispering under his nose. He said, When your mother died, I used to lie awake and listen to the house. The refrigerator. The clock. The wind in the gutter. I thought if I could name every sound, then the silence couldn't swallow me. And then he stopped. It didn't work. I didn't say anything. I remember the house. I remember after she died. The floor would creak in places it hadn't before. Like the wood was learning how to live without her weight. And Dad was walking around in there, just like a man reading a map in a language he forgot. I wanted to tell him that I did the same thing with him. I catalogued the coughs, the sighs, the click of his dentures, the way he said my name when he still knew it. Like each sound was a stone in a river, and I could build a path across. But the river just kept rising.
The monitor beeped. A nurse's shoes squeaked past. Down the hall, someone was crying. A woman, in Spanish. I didn't know what she said, but I recognized it. Dad closed his eyes. He said, Put them on me. They won't fit over your oxygen, I said. Then hold them. So I pressed one to his ear and then the other. I had to cup them with my palms. It was like blessing him. I turned them on. And the hum of the hospital went away. The beeps, the squeaks, the crying, all of it just collapsed into this hush. So complete, it felt like a held breath. He opened his eyes. He said, It's like being underwater. But without the drowning. That's the anti-noise, I said. Anti-noise. He repeated it. Like he was tasting some new medicine. So if I say something, does it cancel that? Only if the microphone hears it. Then don't let it hear me. He lifted his hand. It was trembling. He touched my wrist. I want to tell you something. I leaned in. His voice was like dry leaves. I used to think that silence was the opposite of sound. It's not. Silence is what's left when you stop fighting. I didn't know what to say. I'd spent years fighting. With him, for him, against the slow erasure of his mind. I bought headphones to cancel the world. The world kept coming. It came in the forgetting of my name, then remembering, then forgetting. It came in the bills, the forms, the disinfectant smell. It came in the love. Which is never quiet, even when it's just whispering. Dad, I said, I'm here. He nodded. His eyes drifted shut. I kept holding the headphones to his ears. My arms hurt. The anti-noise hummed, this negative song. I imagined the waves in the air between us. His breath, my breath, the machines. They hit and they cancelled, and what was left was just the shape of what we couldn't say.
I took them off after a while. And the hospital rushed back in. The beeps, the squeaks, the crying. But underneath it, I heard him breathing. Slow, steady. A small, stubborn noise that no machine could cancel. I put the headphones on the nightstand. I didn't turn them on again. I just sat there and listened to my father. And the listening felt like the only thing I ever did right.
